title: KV prefetch & spill postmortem - Acme Labs technical deep dive
summary: Postmortem-style technical deep dive focused on a recent production incident where KV cache spillover caused latency spikes and increased token cost. We walked through eviction telemetry, prefix reuse hotspots, prefetch policy shortcomings, and discussed on-prem/VPC memory constraints. Redwood proposed two prefetch profiles and an experiment plan; Acme agreed to run a targeted benchmark and share traces for further tuning.
next_steps: Redwood (Priya) to export KV telemetry slices and share recommended prefetch config spreadsheet (prefetch-config.xlsx)
Acme to run the supplied benchmark (long-context + burst) and upload logs to shared bucket by 2025-06-12
Schedule follow-up review week of 2025-06-16 to go over results and rollout plan
action_items: Priya Nair; Export KV + paging traces (last 7 days) and annotate eviction storms; 2025-06-09
Tom Reyes; Provide sample user session prefixes that hit long context paths and mark PII-sensitive ones; 2025-06-10
Jordan Kim; Share prefetch-config.xlsx and short runbook for toggling prefetch profiles in Private; 2025-06-08
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-06-05
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Tom Reyes (CTO, Acme), Mei Chen (ML Infra), Samir Patel (Platform), Lena Ortiz (Security)

Auto-summary (auto): Brief postmortem, root cause suspected around aggressive TTL combined with prefix hotspots and prefetch window too narrow; suggested prefetch bump and segmented LRU experiment.

Topics (auto): KV spillover, eviction storms, prefix reuse, prefetch heuristics, on-prem memory caps, quantization effects on memory footprint.

Transcript Body:
00:00:05 Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining we wanted to do a quick postmortem and then get into actionable prefetch ideas, i'll hand off to priya to go over the telemetry she pulled
00:00:22 Priya (Redwood SE): yeah hi all, thanks, uh so we pulled the kv metrics for last week focusing on the long tail bursts you emailed, i flagged three major eviction storms where the prefix collision rate went above 72% which correlates with token latency spikes, note some labels may be slightly off in the export
00:00:45 Mei (Acme): when you say prefix collision can you clarify is that when two user sessions share identical conversation prefix ids or when our client retries are causing duplicate keys?
00:00:58 Priya: good question, here it's mostly prefix reuse across different users — the session prefix hashing they use for multi-tenant routing means frequently used templates (support script, billing faq) end up hot and evict unrelated KV entries, so we see cold starts in the middle of long contexts
00:01:26 Tom (Acme CTO): that matches what we saw — spikes around 11:20 and 18:05 UTC correlated with our support surge, latency jumped from 120ms p50 to near 1.2s p95 and costs went up. we suspected batching misalignment as well
00:01:48 Priya: yep batching was a factor — during the spike, batch sizes shrank because many requests couldn't reuse KV caches and had to recompute kvs, which increases per-token cost and elongates generation time; also we saw a small percentage of memory fragmentation on the on-prem nodes leading to spillback to local SSD paging
00:02:12 Samir (Acme): local SSD paging — is that the private deploy spilling to disk? i thought your runtime kept everything in gpu/gdrm and if full it spills to host memory?
00:02:26 Priya: by default we prefer host memory late-stage spill; in Private you can configure spill policy, but on-prem with limited host RAM and strict SELinux limits we saw spill to local nvme, which causes a big penalty. the on-prem image had quantization set to int8 mixed, but token KV still consumed a fair bit of host ram because of prefix duplication
00:02:55 Lena (Security): any concern about PII landing on NVMe in that spillback flow? we need to know retention/at-rest encryption if that's happening
00:03:06 Jordan: good flag — our Private package encrypts local disk with customer KMS by default if enabled, but some of your nodes didn't have disk encryption toggled in the early rollout — we'll include a checklist for that in the follow-up runbook
00:03:24 Mei: ok thanks. curious about the prefetch window you suggested earlier, what are the tradeoffs if we expand it aggressively?
00:03:36 Priya: expanding prefetch (lookahead KVs) reduces cold starts for long context but increases steady-state memory usage; main knobs are prefetch depth per prefix, LRU window size, and per-prefix TTL. we recommended two profiles: conservative (prefetch depth 2, TTL 20m) and aggressive (depth 6, TTL 60m) as experiments — conservative reduces peak memory but may still see occasional eviction storms; aggressive reduces miss rate but can push you into spill territory on small hosts
00:04:12 Tom: can you explain the eviction storm mechanism once more? like what's the typical sequence we saw in our logs
00:04:21 Priya: sure — sequence we observed: 1) surge of similar prefixes causes many prefetched KV entries to be loaded for those prefixes, 2) host memory saturates, 3) LRU evicts older prefetched entries (which includes active long-context prefixes for other sessions), 4) subsequent requests for those evicted prefixes experience miss -> recompute -> smaller batches, 5) recompute creates more KV churn, spiraling until traffic cools. it's a classic pathological prefix hotspot with positive feedback
00:04:58 Mei: any common mitigation besides increasing host RAM? we don't want to overprovision everywhere
00:05:06 Priya: yes — segmented LRU or per-prefix reservation helps; we suggested a hybrid: reserve a small fraction of KV capacity for high-value prefixes identified by frequency ranking and then evict low-frequency ones first. also soft-TTLs: lower priority prefixes get shorter TTLs so they naturally cycle out without evicting critical long-context entries
00:05:36 Samir: how do we identify high-value prefixes? do we need to sample production traces or can we infer from route metadata?
00:05:44 Priya: best is sampling — frequency and reuse ratio from telemetry; route metadata helps but sometimes templated user prompts map to many variants so sampling is more accurate. we can provide a map file you can ingest into your router to mark reservation candidates
00:06:05 Jordan: also worth calling out quantization interplay — with more aggressive quantization we reduce per-KV size and get more headroom, but we noticed in some models int4/qs8 led to slight quality regressions on rare tokens which matters for legal/regulatory docs you mentioned
00:06:28 Lena: yep, for PII we need to be careful about hallucination/quality regressions. any change to quantization must go through your eval suite and recorded prompts for safety
00:06:40 Priya: agreed — in the proposed experiment we'll keep primary model quant at your current safe setting and only try int4 on a canary replica with strict regression triggers
00:06:51 Tom: back to batching — you talked earlier about batching alignment issues. what's the low hanging fix there?
00:06:59 Priya: often it's request shaping on the client side — try to align max_sequence and pad policies so the runtime can build fuller batches. also enable the KV reuse hint header from the SDK so router groups similar prefixes into same batch window. downside: some clients need code changes
00:07:22 Mei: we can consider SDK changes, but rollout won't be instant. anything at runtime we can toggle?
00:07:29 Priya: yes — the runtime has an experimental 'batch padding window' parameter that waits a configurable ms to collect more compatible requests; raising it from 6ms to 12ms usually increases average batch size with minimal latency tail impact on your traffic mix. we can propose values in the prefetch-config sheet
00:07:49 Jordan: quick pause — i want to call out an operational note: in Private deployments we expose a 'spillback policy' toggle: prefer host ram vs local SSD vs immediate eviction. given your limited host RAM, the recommended path is host-ram-prefer with aggressive reservation on critical prefixes
00:08:07 Samir: if we shift to reservation, what happens on a multi-tenant node where one customer suddenly dominates? do we have cross-tenant fairness?
00:08:18 Priya: reservation is per-customer in our Dedicated offering; in Private it's per-deployment so you control it. cross-tenant fairness becomes more relevant on shared hosts — we can use soft quotas so a tenant can burst but will pay for overcommit.
00:08:40 Mei: any telemetry we should watch in real-time to detect early signs of eviction storms?
00:08:47 Priya: yes — watch prefix miss rate, average batch size, host free memory, and per-prefix reuse ratio. we suggest an alert when prefix miss rate climbs 3x baseline for >2 minutes combined with batch size dropping 30% — that's a leading indicator.
00:09:05 Tom: can you demo where those metrics live in console? i didn't get the dashboard link last time
00:09:11 Jordan: we'll share a dashboard snapshot and the alert rule in the follow-up; i'll add it to next steps
00:09:20 Priya: moving on — we also found a codepath where certain client retries set different session ids which prevented cache key normalization, that's causing apparent duplicate prefixes. long term we recommend normalizing session id at the router and adding a de-dupe layer to client SDKs
00:09:41 Samir: that's actually in our SDK — i can push a patch to normalize session ids for retries, that might help quickly
00:09:49 Mei: good, that patch + conservative prefetch might reduce the immediate pain while we run the aggressive profile in a canary
00:09:57 Tom: timeline question: how long to validate the aggressive prefetch profile safely? 1-2 days?
00:10:05 Priya: for a canary with traffic mirroring, 48 hours gives a good signal for eviction behavior and quality regressions; longer if you want seasonal variance
00:10:15 Jordan: note also the security checklist — Lena, Priya mentioned disk encryption and KMS properly configured on your nodes. we'll include a short checklist and a one-click policy for KMS enablement in the runbook
00:10:29 Lena: please include retention policies for KV dumps — legal needs clarity on how long runtime debugging dumps are kept
00:10:35 Priya: will do.
00:10:40 Priya: next i want to walk through the proposed experiment steps (high level): 1) export baseline traces, 2) enable conservative prefetch on 10% canary, 3) run for 24 hours and capture eviction/latency/cost deltas, 4) if good, enable aggressive on 10% canary with int4 model replica, 5) validate quality and revert if regression
00:11:05 Tom: sounds sensible. what's the rollback plan if the aggressive prefetch causes worse latency?
00:11:11 Priya: rollback is immediate toggling of prefetch depth and TTL in the config; we also keep a quick agent command to flush prefetch state and force recompute, which normally restores baseline behavior quickly — flushing causes temporary spike but prevents ongoing churn
00:11:29 Mei: what about our concern that flushing will expose PII in logs? flushing should not log payloads, right?
:00:11:36 Priya: correct, flush is metadata-only operation we won't persist user content in logs. we'll document that explicitly
00:11:45 Samir: curious — you mentioned segmented LRU. is that something we enable at runtime or a code change to the serving engine?
00:11:52 Priya: segmented LRU exists in runtime as a toggle (experimental), it partitions KV cache into hot/warm/cold segments and moves entries between them based on reuse heuristics. it's not default because some workloads see micro-regressions, but for prefix-hot workloads it's effective
00:12:10 Tom: ok cool. any rough numbers on memory savings with int4 + segmented LRU? ballpark
00:12:17 Priya: we saw 30-45% effective KV-size reduction with int4 plus another 10-15% headroom from segmented LRU in similar customer workloads — but results vary with model and prefix diversity
00:12:33 Mei: if we try this in Private, are there any kernel or driver versions we need to align to avoid host-memory regressions?
00:12:42 Priya: yes — please run the runtime healthcheck we sent earlier; certain older libcuda versions have a known memory fragmentation bug that aggravates spill behavior, we included the list in the checklist
00:12:55 Jordan: ok i want to open to q&a and then recap next steps
00:13:00 Tom: quick question — in the telemetry you sent, i noticed a weird periodicity every ~7 hours, is that maintenance or a job?
00:13:08 Priya: good catch — that aligns with your nightly batch that runs scheduled indexing for some user content which spikes similar prefixes; scheduling that off-peak or throttling prefetch during that job can smooth it out
00:13:25 Samir: we can change that job timing, easy win.
00:13:30 Mei: one more ops question — what logs should we gather for you to triage after we run the canary? full kv dumps or sampled prefixes?
00:13:38 Priya: sampled prefixes and the kv LRU metadata is enough, full dumps are heavy; we provided an export script in the links, use that
00:13:46 Jordan: ok recap: priya will share prefetch-config and telemetry slice; acme will run conservative canary + sdk session-id patch; we'll meet week of 6/16 with results. security checklist to be delivered by 6/08.
00:14:05 Tom: thanks all.
00:14:09 Jordan: thanks, i'll follow up with calendar invite and upload artifacts to the shared bucket

(Above is an excerpt; the call continued with detailed parameter setting and a short live demo around 00:24:00 where Priya toggled a prefetch profile in the Private console.
